What is the publication status on the percentage of non-Hispanic Asian children aged 8–17 with elevated blood pressure, United States, 2013–2014 (NHANES; Table I)?
response_text:
**Suppressed** — it would not be published.

The estimate is 0.9% (SE 0.83; Korn–Graubard 95% CI 0.0–5.1).

Why it fails, under the NCHS Data Presentation Standards for Proportions:

- **Relative CI width = 566.7%**, far above the 130% threshold (table footnote 6). This is the single disqualifying criterion.

What it *passes*, which is why the relative-width rule is the operative one:

- Effective sample size 124.8 (≥ 30), df = 13 (> 8), and the number of events is > 0 and ≠ the denominator — so it clears the sample-size, degrees-of-freedom, and boundary checks.
- Absolute CI width is only 5.1 percentage points, which looks acceptable in isolation; the standards require examining relative width precisely because a small absolute width can still be enormous relative to a near-zero estimate.

Two related points:

- **The complement is presented.** Normal or borderline blood pressure for non-Hispanic Asian children (99.1%) has the same absolute CI width (5.1 points) but a relative CI width under 130%, so it *would* be published — carrying a footnote (footnote 7) indicating that its complement does not meet presentation standards.
- **Contrast with the older RSE rule.** RSE here is 92.2%, so this estimate would also have been suppressed under an RSE > 30% criterion. The instructive case in the table is the opposite direction: non-Hispanic white elevated (0.5%, RSE 58.0%) is *presentable* under the proportions standards but would have been suppressed under RSE > 30%.
